extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and policymakers interested in the Volkswagen emissions scandal and vehicle emissions regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, regulatory requirements and evaluation criteria for automotive diesel emissions, recall plans, fixes and remediation as discussed in the Volkswagen 'Dieselgate' coverage. Covers testing protocols, recall approval processes, consumer compensation and legal/penalty metrics across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal EU emissions compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures (software or hardware fixes) must achieve legal EU emissions compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volkswagen stated its proposed solutions would be designed to achieve legal EU emissions compliance without impairing engine performance or consumption; regulators require fixes that bring vehicles into conformity with applicable EU emission limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impairing engine performance or fuel consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Emissions fixes should preserve engine output and fuel economy where feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: VW and executives repeatedly asserted fixes would preserve fuel economy ratings though some tests (e.g., Auto Motor und Sport; Teknikens Värld) later showed reductions in power output or increases in fuel consumption; regulators (e.g., CARB) consider overall impacts on performance when approving fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of selective catalytic reduction (SCR) technology where required
rubrics_metrics.description: Transition to SCR or similar after-treatment technologies as a strategy to improve diesel emissions and meet standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volkswagen announced plans to switch 'as soon as possible' to the use of selective catalytic reduction technology in Europe and North America to improve diesel emissions; regulators may expect adoption of technically appropriate after-treatment solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall plan submission, approval and deadlines (KBA example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers must submit recall plans to the competent authority by specified deadlines and obtain approval before proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KBA required Volkswagen to send a recall plan before end of October for 2.0‑litre cars and before end of November for 1.2 and 1.6‑litre cars; if KBA approves a plan, Volkswagen can then start handling the cars. Authorities required removal of the illegal software and assurance that emission rules are fulfilled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory requirement to remove illegal 'defeat device' software
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities require removal of software classified as an illegal defeat device and restoration of legal compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KBA views the software as illegal and ordered a full recall; German authorities require Volkswagen to remove the software and ensure emission rules are fulfilled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall fixes must deliver compliance across real-world conditions and temperature ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Approved fixes must reduce emissions under the range of normal operating conditions (including temperature ranges) and not only in narrow test conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A district court later ruled an updated software didn't properly address emissions, citing a Tiguan engine that only reduced emissions in the ambient temperature range of 10–32 °C (50–90 °F). Regulators have tested vehicles both in laboratory and on-road (PEMS) to assess real-world compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory testing methodology: laboratory vs real-world (PEMS) and realistic driving emissions tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Emissions evaluation should rely on realistic driving test procedures (on‑road PEMS and more realistic EU driving tests) rather than solely on laboratory cycles that can be gamed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The European Parliament urged tougher, more 'realistic' emissions tests; regulators tested vehicles in laboratory and on-road with PEMS after concerns that lab tests understated NOx emissions. Legislation later moved toward real-world conformity checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure and certification of emissions-related software to authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers must disclose emissions-related software to certifying authorities (EPA, CARB, etc.) as part of emissions certification; failure to disclose can lead to withdrawal of certification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the US Volkswagen withdrew its application for emissions certification for 2016 diesel models; EPA quarantined some 2016 models until it was clear their catalysts behave the same on road as in tests. Regulators expect truthful, timely disclosure of software affecting emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: CARB criterion for acceptable recall plans
rubrics_metrics.description: CARB requires that recall plans 'adequately address overall impacts on vehicle performance, emissions and safety'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: US regulators rejected Volkswagen's recall plans for 2.0‑litre engines on the grounds that they 'do not adequately address overall impacts on vehicle performance, emissions and safety', indicating multi-dimensional evaluation of fixes beyond emissions levels alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory authority power to check conformity and recall vehicles (EU commission right)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities have the power to check vehicle conformity to emission standards and to order recalls where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From September 2020, European Union laws gave the European Commission the right to check car conformity to emission standards and to recall vehicles when needed; fines can be levied per car.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial penalties per vehicle and jurisdictional fines
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalties for non-compliance can include per-vehicle fines and large aggregate fines imposed by national or supranational authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA noted potential fines up to US$37,500 per vehicle; EU laws allow fines up to €30,000 per car. The page also references jurisdictional fines/sentences such as Germany's €1 billion fine, Canada's CA$196.5M, Australia's A$125M, Brazil's ordered R$1,000,000,000 payment, illustrating fines vary by jurisdiction and legal basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal and civil liability for executives and companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives and companies can face criminal investigations, prosecutions, and civil lawsuits arising from emissions violations and related misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents prosecutors' investigations, raids, charges against executives (e.g., Winterkorn, Stadler), criminal probes in multiple countries, and thousands of civil suits by consumers seeking compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer remediation options and settlement structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Remediation for affected vehicle owners can include buybacks, repairs, replacement vehicles, vouchers, cash payments, and claims funds managed under settlement agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: VW offered US$2,000 trade‑in offers, US$1,000 vouchers to some owners, and a claims fund to provide full compensation packages (cash, buy‑backs, repairs or replacement cars). Courts and mediators (e.g., appointed mediator Robert Mueller) oversaw settlements that included buybacks for nearly 500,000 2.0‑litre vehicles in North America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely information to consumers about fixes and compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers must provide timely, clear information to consumers about recall steps, repairs and compensation options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The European Union warned Volkswagen that it was not moving fast enough to issue repairs and to provide consumers with appropriate information on what steps were being taken and what compensation was being offered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulators may broaden investigations to other models and manufacturers
rubrics_metrics.description: Detection of defeat devices can trigger widened probes across additional models and other manufacturers' vehicles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA broadened investigations to 28 diesel‑powered models by other manufacturers; national authorities (e.g., KBA) tested cars from different manufacturers both in laboratory and on-road with PEMS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall implementation strategy must account for engine variants and repair variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recall rollouts should be phased and tailored to clusters of engines/models because multiple engine sizes and many variations to repairs may exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volkswagen rolled out recalls in waves for clusters (three sizes of affected diesel engines and more than a dozen variations to the repairs), with the first model (Amarok) repaired before larger-volume models; timelines differed by engine size in the UK and elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate governance and monitoring obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies have a duty to monitor employees and internal processes; failure to supervise employees who modified software can result in corporate fines and sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Germany imposed a €1 billion fine on Volkswagen for failing to monitor the employees that modified the software behind the scandal; regulators and courts scrutinize corporate oversight practices when violations occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory basis for consumer claims (e.g., false advertising, misleading representations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers may be liable under consumer protection laws and advertising statutes for misleading claims about vehicle emissions and environmental benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The US Federal Trade Commission sued Volkswagen for false advertising due to fraudulent promotional claims. Australia fined Volkswagen for making false and misleading representations about compliance with diesel emissions standards.
